<Rep. Nydia M. Velázquez>: The U.S. Small Business Administration (SBA)'s disaster loan program provides low-interest direct loans to help businesses, nonprofits, homeowners, and renters recover from a declared disaster.\1\ The disaster loan program has four major lending programs: (1) real property disaster for households;
(2) personal property for households; (3) physical disaster business loans for businesses of all sizes, and (4) economic injury disaster loans (EIDLs) for small businesses and nonprofits. Additionally, disaster loans can be increased for mitigation purposes and can be used to help small businesses with operating expenses for an employee on active-duty leave.
\1\See U.S. Small Bus. Admin., Off. of Disaster Assistance, https:/ /www.sba.gov/funding-programs/disaster-assistance (last visited Aug. 10, 2022).
From July to October 2024, several major hurricanes made landfall in the United States, leading up to the SBA's announcement on October 15, 2024, that funds in its disaster loans program account had been exhausted. The SBA could not approve and disburse new loans until the Congress appropriated additional funds on December 21, 2024, via the American Relief Act of 2025.
The SBA has existing reporting requirements on the disaster program that they failed at the time to submit, including a monthly estimate on the number of days of funding remining in the account. The authorizing and appropriating committees were notified of the impending funding shortage, but not with enough time to act before it ran out. A lack of communication and a series of compounding disasters depleted the disaster account faster than anticipated when the House was not in session throughout October, leading to a prolonged lapse of funding.
Nydia M. Velazquez,
Ranking Member.
